chunks: Multiphase vs single-phase trade-offs. The question: What are the pros/cons/tradeoffs vs single-phase buck converters?
Going from one phase to several buys you more current, lower and faster ripple, quicker response to load steps and heat spread over more parts.
It costs money, board area and control complexity. So multiphase is a trade, not an upgrade for every design.
You can move a heavy load with one huge truck or with four small vans. The truck needs one big engine and one driver, but all the heat and wear sits in one place.
The vans share the load and are easier to cool and replace, but need four drivers who must coordinate.
The picture breaks down on one point: splitting the current does not by itself cut the heat from resistance.
Four small stages with the same total switch size as one big stage lose about the same.
Capacitance needed to hold a 20 millivolts sag for a 30 amps step in the ideal slew-limited case, with 300 nanohenries per phase.
Doubling the phases halves the capacitance, with diminishing absolute returns beyond four to six phases.
A real design also needs enough ESR/ESL budget and a fast loop, so this is a trend rather than a BOM.
Phase: one complete buck stage, with its own inductor and pair of switches (FETs) ("What a multiphase buck is").
Effective inductance: the combined inductance seen by a load step, L over N . Phase shedding: switching off phases at light load to save power ("Multiphase impact on efficiency").
Fixed losses: power each running phase spends every cycle whatever the load, such as driving its switches; they add up with every active phase.
Current sensing: measuring each phase's current so the controller can balance them.
A processor rail needs 60 amps. One stage would carry all 60 amps in one hot spot. Four phases carry 15 amps each, so each part is easier to buy and cool.
The price is four inductors, four pairs of FETs and a multiphase controller. Now look at light load: say each phase wastes 0. 1 watts in fixed losses, and the load is 5 watts.
Four phases lose 0. 4 watts, so efficiency is 5 over 5. 4 about 93 % , while one phase gives 5 over 5. 1 about 98 % . That is the whole idea.
"Multiphase gives you more current, lower and higher-frequency output ripple, a faster transient response because the effective inductance is L over N, and heat spread over several stages.
The costs are more parts and area, a more complex controller with current balancing, fixed losses that multiply with the phase count, and a harder layout.
At the same total silicon the conduction loss doesn't change, so I'd pick multiphase for high-current, low-voltage rails with tough transients, and stay single-phase for low-current rails."
